extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature (readers of Milton)
extracted.subtask_description: Edition introduction and facsimile text of John Milton's Areopagitica (arguments against press licensing), aimed at readers and students of English literature and intellectual history. Contains editorial notes, historical context, and Milton's normative claims about censorship, liberty, and the value of books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to pre-publication licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Book, pamphlet, or paper shall be henceforth Printed unlesse the same be first approved and licenct by such, or at least one of such as shall be thereto appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues this order (pre-publication licensing) is novel, derived from the Inquisition, and should be resisted: licensing is a prior restraint that originated with tyrannous ecclesiastical authorities and is inappropriate for a free commonwealth. The edition's introduction repeatedly frames the licensing clause as the principal target of Milton's 'Homily' and situates it historically (e.g., imprimatur practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates should notice only blasphemous or libellous writings
rubrics_metrics.description: In Athens... I finde but only two sorts of writings which the Magistrate car'd to take notice of: those either blasphemous and Atheisticall, or Libellous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton uses ancient practice (Athens, Rome) as a model: civil authorities intervened chiefly against writings that denied the gods or defamed individuals. Other controversial, licentious, or philosophic works were generally left unread or tolerated. Examples cited: Protagoras condemned for atheism; comedies and Epicurean writings often left alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punish genuinely dangerous works, not preemptively censor all
rubrics_metrics.description: If it prov'd a Monster, who denies but that it was justly burnt, or sunk into the Sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton concedes that clearly harmful works (monstrous blasphemies or active seditions) may be justly destroyed or punished after identification; the argument opposes blanket prior restraint and supports targeted action against concrete harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books are living and must be preserved (value of books)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are not absolutely 'dead' things, but doe contain a potencie of life in them... who destroys a good Booke, kills reason it selfe, kills the Image of God as it were in the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton frames books as repositories of living intellect and moral/political value ('the pretious life-blood of a master spirit'). This is used as a normative criterion for treatment of books: they merit protection because destroying them destroys reason, cultural memory, and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing will not suppress scandalous, seditious, and libellous books
rubrics_metrics.description: That this Order avails nothing to the suppressing of scandalous, seditious, and libellous Books, which were mainly intended to be supprest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues that licensing is ineffective at its ostensible purpose of stopping libel and sedition; historical examples are marshalled to show censorship often misses its targets or is co-opted. This functions as an argument against licensing as a remedy for those specific evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing discourages learning and hinders the discovery of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be primely to the discouragement of all learning, and the stop of Truth, not only by the disexercising and blunting our abilities in what we know already, but by hindring and cropping the discovery that might bee yet further made both in religious and civill Wisdome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton claims prior restraint dulls intellectual capacities and prevents future discoveries in religion and civil wisdom. This is a broad quality criterion: policies that chill publication harm the progress of knowledge and public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer retrospective examination/punishment over prior authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: He was 'often employed to report on papers or pamphlets after they were published' — to officially review them in fact; but not to authorize or license them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text endorses the practice of examining and (if necessary) punishing writings after publication rather than requiring pre-publication approval. This preserves freedom of expression while allowing accountability for genuinely harmful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical imprimatur/approval is procedural censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: No Book... should be Printed unlesse it were approv'd and licen't under the hands of 2 or 3 glutton Friers... Imprimatur... If it seem good to the reverend Master of the holy Palace...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton reproduces examples of ecclesiastical approval forms (imprimatur) to show how church procedure functioned as prior restraint. He criticizes the reliance on Latin/formal stamps and the Romanizing attitude that made such approvals a gatekeeping procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: True civil liberty requires free complaint, deep consideration, and speedy reform
rubrics_metrics.description: When complaints are freely heard, deeply considered, and speedily reform'd, then is the utmost bound of civill liberty attain'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a standard for governance of the press and polity: freedom should include capacity for criticism and institutional responsiveness. It justifies tolerant publication practices by coupling liberty with mechanisms for redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion of institutions invented by oppressors (bad provenance makes a practice suspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: If that thing... falsest seducers and oppressors of men were the first who tooke it up, and to no other purpose but to obstruct and hinder the first approach of Reformation, I am of those who beleeve it will be a harder alchymy then Lullius ever knew, to sublimat any good use out of such an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton urges skepticism toward practices (like licensing) that originated with tyrannical or oppressive institutions (e.g., the Inquisition). The provenance and historical purpose of a regulatory measure count as criteria in judging whether it should be adopted.
